title: Deepfake Fraud in 2027: Emerging Threats, Biometric Defenses, and What Organizations Need to Know
summary: Explore deepfake fraud trends for 2027, including AI impersonation, injection attacks, synthetic identities, and how biometrics and liveness detection help.
body_markdown:
Deepfake fraud is entering a new phase, and for organizations preparing for 2027, the challenge is no longer simply recognizing AI-generated images, videos, or voices. It’s establishing whether the person behind a digital interaction is real, physically present, and who they claim to be.


Generative AI has fundamentally changed the economics of identity fraud. Techniques that once required specialized expertise and significant resources are becoming increasingly accessible, allowing attackers to create convincing synthetic identities, impersonate legitimate users, and automate attacks at scale.


The consequences are already being felt. According to[Aware’s 2026 State of Biometric Security in the Age of AI Fraud report](https://www.aware.com/resource/biometric-security-in-the-age-of-ai-fraud-report/) , 44% of surveyed organizations experienced AI-related fraud within the previous year. Meanwhile,[Entrust’s 2026 Identity Fraud Report](https://www.entrust.com/resources/reports/identity-fraud-report) found that deepfakes accounted for one in five biometric fraud attempts, while injection attacks increased 40% year over year.


As organizations look toward 2027, these developments point to an important shift: identity security can no longer depend solely on whether credentials, documents, or digital representations appear legitimate. It must establish confidence in the human behind the interaction.


## The Deepfake Fraud Tactics Organizations Should Watch in 2027


Deepfake technology continues to evolve, but the most consequential developments are not necessarily the most visually impressive. Attackers are increasingly combining synthetic media with techniques designed to exploit weaknesses throughout the identity verification process.


Several tactics deserve particular attention.


### Real-Time Deepfake and Voice Impersonation


AI-generated video and voice cloning are making impersonation attacks increasingly convincing during live interactions. Criminals can use these technologies to impersonate executives, customers, government officials, or other trusted individuals during video calls, account recovery requests, and financial transactions.


Unlike prerecorded deepfakes, real-time impersonation can respond dynamically during a conversation, making it harder for employees or traditional verification processes to identify deception.


The FBI has already[warned](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260720) about criminals using AI-generated video to impersonate government and law enforcement officials. As these capabilities become more accessible, organizations should expect greater pressure on processes that rely on visual familiarity or voice recognition alone.


### Injection Attacks that Bypass the Camera


One of the most significant emerging threats targets the verification infrastructure itself.


In a traditional presentation attack, a fraudster might hold a photograph, mask, or video recording in front of a camera. An[injection attack](https://www.aware.com/blog-defending-biometric-systems-against-injection-attacks/) , however, bypasses the normal capture process by introducing manipulated or synthetic biometric data directly into an application or video stream. Attackers may exploit virtual cameras, device emulators, modified applications, or compromised devices to make fabricated content appear as though it originated from a legitimate camera.


This distinction matters because a biometric system cannot rely exclusively on analyzing what appears in an image. It must also consider whether the image came from an authentic capture event.


### AI-Generated Documents and Synthetic Identity Fraud


Synthetic identity fraud combines fabricated and sometimes stolen personal information to construct identities that may not belong to any real individual. Generative AI makes these attacks more sophisticated by enabling criminals to create realistic facial images, counterfeit identity documents, and supporting digital information that appear consistent. These fabricated identities may be used to open financial accounts, apply for benefits, obtain credentials, or establish identities that can later be exploited.


The challenge extends beyond detecting fake documents. Organizations must verify that the individual presenting those documents is genuine, that the identity information is trustworthy, and that the person is authorized to complete the requested action.


### Automated, Scalable Identity Attacks


Perhaps the most consequential trend heading into 2027 is the increasing automation of fraud.


AI-assisted tools, fraud-as-a-service offerings, and automated testing can allow attackers to generate numerous identity variations and repeatedly test verification systems for weaknesses. Rather than relying on one convincing deepfake, fraudsters can systematically explore which identities, devices, or verification processes are most vulnerable.


For defenders, this changes the operational equation. Fraud prevention systems must be capable of adapting to new techniques without lengthy replacement or integration cycles.


## How Biometrics and Liveness Detection Help Prevent Deepfake Fraud


As synthetic content becomes harder to distinguish from authentic media, biometric[identity verification](https://www.aware.com/identity-verification-software/) provides an important foundation for connecting digital activity to human identity.


Facial recognition, fingerprint recognition, and other biometric modalities can help establish whether an individual matches a trusted identity record. But biometric matching alone is insufficient when attackers can manipulate or fabricate the biometric samples submitted for verification.


This is where[liveness detection](https://www.aware.com/blog-liveness-detection-explained/) becomes essential.


Liveness detection is a biometric security capability that helps determine whether a biometric sample is being captured from a real, living person physically present during verification. It is a subset of presentation attack detection (PAD), a broader category of technologies designed to distinguish legitimate biometric interactions from spoofing attempts involving photographs, masks, replayed videos, and other deceptive materials. Active liveness detection may require users to complete challenges or movements, while[passive liveness](https://www.aware.com/passive-liveness-detection-is-the-secret-to-stopping-fraud-blog/) detection analyzes signals without requiring explicit user actions. Both approaches can support fraud prevention, depending on the implementation and threats being addressed.


However, increasingly sophisticated injection attacks require organizations to look beyond conventional liveness detection. Modern defenses may incorporate injection attack detection, camera integrity checks, device analysis, and other mechanisms designed to verify the authenticity of the capture process itself.


Independent evaluations also matter. Standards and testing frameworks such as ISO/IEC 30107-3 for presentation attack detection and CEN/TS 18099 for injection attack detection help organizations assess whether biometric defenses perform against relevant attack methods.


The goal is not to rely on one algorithm to detect every possible deepfake. It is to establish multiple complementary layers of confidence in the person, the biometric sample, and the capture process.


## Deepfake Fraud Risks Across Key Industries


Although deepfake fraud affects nearly every digitally connected organization, the consequences and highest-risk interactions differ by industry.


### Banking and Fintech: Protecting the Entire Customer Lifecycle


For financial institutions, deepfake and synthetic identity fraud threaten customer onboarding, account access, payment authorization, and account recovery. A synthetic identity may successfully open an account, while a deepfake impersonation attempt could target an established customer during a high-value transaction or credential reset.


Banks and fintech providers should therefore consider biometric verification and liveness detection throughout the customer lifecycle, applying stronger assurance when transaction risk increases. Combining biometrics with document verification, device intelligence, and behavioral or transactional risk signals can help institutions detect suspicious activity while preserving low-friction experiences for legitimate customers.


### Government and Public Sector: Strengthening Digital Identity Assurance


Government agencies increasingly depend on remote identity verification to deliver citizen services, administer benefits, support workforce access, and protect sensitive information. Deepfake and synthetic identity attacks create risks ranging from fraudulent enrollment to impersonation of legitimate beneficiaries or government personnel.


Biometric matching and liveness detection can help agencies strengthen identity proofing and authentication while reducing reliance on vulnerable knowledge-based verification methods.


Importantly, security must be balanced with accessibility, privacy, and equitable access to essential services. Risk-based identity workflows, appropriate human review, and independently evaluated technologies can help agencies strengthen assurance without creating unnecessary barriers for legitimate users.


### Travel and National Security: Establishing Trust at Scale


In aviation, border management, and national security environments, accurate identity verification is essential for both security and operational efficiency. As digital travel credentials, remote enrollment, automated checkpoints, and biometric passenger processing expand, organizations must protect against fraudulent identities and manipulated biometric submissions.


Liveness detection, biometric matching, and secure capture technologies can help establish confidence that a traveler or individual is genuinely present and matches the identity being asserted.


For these environments, speed and accuracy are equally important. Effective defenses must support high-assurance decisions without introducing bottlenecks that undermine passenger throughput or mission-critical operations.


## Building a More Adaptive Deepfake Defense Strategy for 2027


The organizations best positioned to confront deepfake fraud in 2027 will be those that move beyond isolated verification technologies toward a coordinated, risk-based identity strategy. That means treating identity assurance as an ongoing process rather than a single checkpoint at onboarding.


It also requires connecting biometric matching, liveness detection, injection attack prevention, document verification, and contextual risk signals so they contribute to more informed identity decisions.


[Biometric orchestration](https://www.aware.com/blog-biometric-orchestration-intelligence-layer/) can play an important role by allowing organizations to coordinate multiple identity technologies, evaluate vendor performance, adjust verification workflows, and respond to emerging threats without rebuilding their entire infrastructure.


> As fraud techniques evolve, flexibility becomes a security capability in its own right.


Ultimately, the challenge heading into 2027 is not whether organizations can identify every convincing deepfake. It is whether their identity infrastructure can consistently distinguish legitimate human interactions from fraudulent ones, even as the methods of deception change.
